5 Uniformly accelerated motion in vector form

html:
The big picture

Lecture 4 went down the chain position → velocity → acceleration by differentiating. This lecture goes back up by integrating: velocity = starting velocity + the integral of the acceleration, position = starting position + the integral of the velocity. The values at the start, the initial state x_0, v_0, are what the integrals can't know. For constant acceleration (uniformly accelerated motion) the integrals give v = v_0 + at and x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2, and eliminating t gives the time-free relation v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\,(x - x_0). Free fall is the case \vec a = \vec g, the same for every mass; falling from rest through a height H gives the Torricelli equation v = \sqrt{2gH}. If a changes with time, only the integrals work. In vector form, each coordinate of a uniformly accelerated motion is a parabola in t. Seen from a moving point, positions, velocities and accelerations are differences (relative motion).

1 Motion at constant acceleration

Lecture: the lecture handout p. 1 ("1D") – p. 2 (top) · Giancoli §2-5

Many motions have, at least for a while, a constant acceleration: a car speeding up evenly, a train braking, a falling stone. For these, velocity and position can be written as simple formulas of time. The lecture gets them by running the derivatives of lecture 4 backwards.

Velocity. The acceleration is the derivative of the velocity, a = \mathrm dv/\mathrm dt. Integrate both sides from the starting time t_0 to a time t:

\begin{aligned} \int_{t_0}^{t} \frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm d\tau}\,\mathrm d\tau &= \int_{t_0}^{t} a(\tau)\,\mathrm d\tau && \text{(integrate } a = \mathrm dv/\mathrm d\tau \text{ from } t_0 \text{ to } t) \\ v(t) - v(t_0) &= \int_{t_0}^{t} a(\tau)\,\mathrm d\tau && \text{(fundamental theorem of calculus)} \\ v(t) &= v_0 + \int_{t_0}^{t} a(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau && \text{(add } v(t_0) = v_0) \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • v(t) — velocity along the line at time t (m/s); its sign gives the direction
  • v_0 = v(t_0) — velocity at the starting time t_0 (m/s), part of the initial state
  • a(\tau) — acceleration (m/s²), possibly changing with time
  • \tau — integration variable (s), a time running from t_0 to t (Greek "tau")

The board starts with the last line. The upper limit is called t, so the variable inside the integral needs another name, \tau. In words: the velocity now = the velocity at the start + all the small changes a\,\mathrm d\tau since then (the area under the a–t graph). The integral gives only the change; v_0 must come from the problem.

With a = \text{const} and t_0 = 0\,\mathrm s (board), the constant comes out of the integral and \int_0^t 1\,\mathrm d\tau = t:

v(t) = v_0 + a\,t

Symbols as above, a now constant. The velocity grows linearly with time: a straight line in the v–t graph, starting at v_0 with slope a.

Position. The same argument one level up, with v = \mathrm dx/\mathrm dt:

x(t) = x_0 + \int_{t_0}^{t} v(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau
Symbols
  • x(t) — position along the line at time t (m); x_0 = x(t_0) — starting position (m)
  • v(\tau) — velocity at the time \tau (m/s)

Insert v(\tau) = v_0 + a\tau (with t_0 = 0):

\begin{aligned} x(t) &= x_0 + \int_0^t (v_0 + a\,\tau)\,\mathrm d\tau && \text{(insert the velocity)} \\ &= x_0 + v_0\,\tau\Big|_0^t + a\,\frac{\tau^2}{2}\Big|_0^t && \text{(integrate term by term, power rule)} \\ &= x_0 + v_0\,t + \tfrac12\,a\,t^2 && \text{(insert the limits; the lower limit gives 0)} \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. The board boxes the result:

\boxed{\,x(t) = x_0 + v_0 \cdot t + \tfrac12\,a\,t^2\,}
Symbols
  • x(t) — position at time t (m); x_0 — starting position (m); v_0 — starting velocity (m/s)
  • a — the constant acceleration (m/s²); t — time since the start (s)

The three terms: where you started (x_0) + how far you would get at the starting velocity (v_0 t) + the extra due to the acceleration (\tfrac12 a t^2). The \tfrac12 is the triangle under the rising v–t line: base t, height at, area \tfrac12 \cdot t \cdot at. Next to the box the board writes v = v_0 and v(t) = v_0 + a \cdot t (underlined), with an arrow to the next step.

Unclear (p. 2): "v = v_0"

The line v = v_0 stands beside v(t) = v_0 + a\cdot t without a condition. It is only true at t = 0 (or when a = 0). It is transcribed as written; the arrow shows the board is about to use v(t) = v_0 + at.

Eliminating the time. Many problems give a distance and ask for a speed, or the reverse, and never mention a time: "how fast after falling 20 m?", "how long is the braking distance from 100 km/h?". One equation linking v and x directly does this. The board solves the velocity law for t (curved arrow) and inserts it into the box:

t = \bigl(v(t) - v_0\bigr)/a
x(t) - x_0 = v_0\,\frac{v(t) - v_0}{a} + \frac{\bigl(v(t) - v_0\bigr)^2}{2a} = \frac{v^2(t) - v_0^2}{2a}
Symbols
  • a — constant acceleration, a \neq 0; x(t) - x_0 — displacement since the start (m); other symbols as above

The single "=" in the second line hides these steps (writing v for v(t)):

\begin{aligned} x - x_0 &= v_0\,\frac{v - v_0}{a} + \tfrac12\,a\,\frac{(v - v_0)^2}{a^2} && \text{(insert } t \text{ into } v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2) \\ &= \frac{2v_0\,(v - v_0) + (v - v_0)^2}{2a} && \text{(cancel one } a\text{; common denominator } 2a) \\ &= \frac{(v - v_0)\,(2v_0 + v - v_0)}{2a} && \text{(factor out } v - v_0) \\ &= \frac{(v - v_0)(v + v_0)}{2a} = \frac{v^2 - v_0^2}{2a} && \text{(third binomial formula)} \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. Multiply by 2a and add v_0^2:

v^2(x) = v_0^2 + 2a\,\bigl(x(t) - x_0\bigr)
Symbols
  • v^2(x) — squared velocity (m²/s²) when the body is at position x; "(x)" because time no longer appears; other symbols as above

Special case v_0 = 0\,\mathrm{m/s}, x_0 = 0\,\mathrm{m} (board): the v_0^2 term and x_0 vanish, and the arrow under "x(t)" points out that it is now just "x", the distance from the start, reached from rest:

v^2 = 2a\,x(t) = 2a\,x

Symbols as above.

On 16 Oct the board writes the same law in a form used for any two moments of a motion:

v_1^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\,s

with "v_1 fixed": v_1 = v(t = \ldots\,\mathrm s), v_0 = v(t = 0\,\mathrm s), a = acceleration = const, and a "?" under s. Board sketch: a v–t graph, a straight line rising from v_0 at t = 0 to v_1 at a later time (dashed).

Symbols
  • v_1 — velocity at the later moment of interest (m/s); "fixed" = one chosen moment, whose time is left open
  • v_0 — velocity at t = 0\,\mathrm s (m/s); a — constant acceleration (m/s²)
  • s — the displacement between the two moments (m)

The "?" asks exactly what s is: the displacement x - x_0 from the moment with v_0 to the moment with v_1, not a position. The straight v–t line is what "a = \text{const}" looks like.

Intuition

Choosing among the three formulas is about which quantity is missing from the problem. v = v_0 + at has no position; x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2 has no final velocity; v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\,\Delta x has no time. Pick the one that doesn't contain the quantity you neither know nor want.

Common mistake — the constant-acceleration formulas when a is not constant

All three formulas were derived from a = \text{const}. If a changes with time (a motor ramping up, drag growing with speed), go back to the integrals (section 4). Also check the start: the formulas assume the clock starts at t_0 = 0 with the initial state x_0, v_0.

Connection

The prep course had these formulas as given (1 Kinematics › Simple motions on a line); here they are derived from the integrals (4.1 Integral Calculus › Distance from velocity). Forward pointer: multiplying v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\,\Delta x by m/2 turns it into the work–energy relation (10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy).

2 Solving problems with constant acceleration

Lecture: p. 3 (class exercise 1), p. 7 (car overtaking a train) · Giancoli §2-6

Problem-solving steps — constant acceleration in one dimension
  1. Decide which body and which time interval; start the clock at t = 0 at the beginning of it.
  2. Sketch the situation; choose the origin and which direction is positive.
  3. List what is given and what is wanted, at the start and at the end; translate words ("from rest" → v_0 = 0, "stops" → v = 0). Give every vector quantity its sign.
  4. Check that a is constant over the interval; pick the formula that lacks the quantity you neither know nor want.
  5. Solve algebraically first, then insert numbers with units. A quadratic gives two roots: keep the one that fits the situation (usually t > 0).
  6. Check units, sign and size; cross-check with a second formula.
Worked example — braking distance

A trolley rolls at v_0 = 20\,\mathrm{m/s} and brakes uniformly with a = -5\,\mathrm{m/s^2} until it stops. How far does it go, and how long does it take?

  1. Pick the formula from what is asked: a distance, no time given → v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\,(x - x_0).
  2. Stopped means v = 0: 0 = 20^2 + 2\cdot(-5)\,(x - x_0), so x - x_0 = \dfrac{-400}{-10}\,\mathrm{m} = 40\,\mathrm{m}.
  3. Time from v = v_0 + at: 0 = 20 - 5\,t, so t = 4\,\mathrm{s}.
  4. Check with the position law: 20 \cdot 4 - \tfrac12 \cdot 5 \cdot 4^2 = 80 - 40 = 40\,\mathrm{m} ✓. The acceleration is negative because it points against v_0.

Class exercise 1: UALM – 1D linear motion

Task (sheet): Consider a 1D reference frame. A car starts from the origin with initial positive velocity v_0 and it is subject to a negative acceleration -a_0. a) Compute the maximum distance reached. b) Compute the time t_1 at which the car stops. c) Compute the time t_2 at which the car passes back through the origin. d) Compute the car's velocity at t = t_2.

"UALM" means uniformly accelerated linear motion. The car moves forward (v_0 > 0) while the acceleration points backwards (-a_0, with a_0 > 0 its size): it brakes, stops and, since the acceleration keeps acting, rolls back. The board writes the acceleration as a and inserts a = -a_0 only at the end of each line. It starts from the two laws with x_0 = 0 ("starts from the origin") and t_0 = 0:

x(t) = v_0\cdot t + \frac12\,a\,t^2, \qquad v(t) = v_0 + a\cdot t

Symbols as in section 1. The board answers b) before a), because the maximum distance is reached exactly when the car stops.

b) Stop. "Stops" means velocity zero; subtract v_0, divide by a, insert a = -a_0:

v(t_s) = 0 = v_0 + a\cdot t_s \quad\Rightarrow\quad t_s = -\frac{v_0}{a} = -\frac{v_0}{-a_0} = \frac{v_0}{a_0}
Symbols
  • t_s — the stopping time ("stop"), the task's t_1 (s); a_0 > 0 — size of the braking acceleration (m/s²)

The two minus signs cancel: t_s > 0, as a time after the start must be.

a) Maximum distance. Before t_s the car moves forward, after it moves back, so the farthest point is where it turns:

\begin{aligned} x(t_s) &= v_0\left(-\frac{v_0}{a}\right) + \tfrac12\,a\left(-\frac{v_0}{a}\right)^2 && \text{(insert } t_s = -v_0/a) \\ &= -\frac{v_0^2}{a} + \frac{v_0^2}{2a} && \text{(square removes the sign; cancel one } a) \\ &= -\frac12\,\frac{v_0^2}{a} = \frac12\,\frac{v_0^2}{a_0} && \text{(}-1 + \tfrac12 = -\tfrac12\text{; insert } a = -a_0) \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. Check with the time-free law: 0 = v_0^2 + 2(-a_0)\,x_\text{max} gives the same x_\text{max} = v_0^2/(2a_0) ✓.

c) Back at the origin (t_r = t_2, "return"): x = 0 again. Factor out t_r; a product is zero when one factor is zero, so either t_r = 0 (the start) or the bracket is zero (the board marks both with "= 0"):

x(t_r) = 0 = v_0\cdot t_r + \frac12\cdot a\cdot t_r^2 = t_r\Bigl(v_0 + \frac12\,a\,t_r\Bigr) \quad\Rightarrow\quad t_r = -\frac{2v_0}{a} = \frac{2v_0}{a_0}

Symbols as above. Note t_2 = 2\,t_s: the trip back takes as long as the trip out.

d) Velocity there. Insert t_2 = -2v_0/a; the a cancels:

v(t_2) = v_0 + a\cdot t_2 = v_0 + a\Bigl(-\frac{2v_0}{a}\Bigr) = -v_0

Symbols as above. The car comes back with the speed it left with, now moving towards negative x. Check with the time-free law: at x = 0, v^2 = v_0^2 ✓.

Worked example — the same exercise with numbers

v_0 = 10\,\mathrm{m/s}, a_0 = 2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}.

  1. Stop: t_s = 10/2 = 5\,\mathrm s.
  2. Maximum distance: x_\text{max} = \tfrac12 \cdot 100/2 = 25\,\mathrm m. Check: 10 \cdot 5 - \tfrac12 \cdot 2 \cdot 25 = 25\,\mathrm m ✓.
  3. Back at the origin: t_2 = 2 \cdot 10/2 = 10\,\mathrm s = 2\,t_s.
  4. Velocity there: v(10\,\mathrm s) = 10 - 2 \cdot 10 = -10\,\mathrm{m/s} = -v_0 ✓.

Example: car overtaking a train (solve at home)

Board sketch (p. 7): at t = 0 a car with v_C = 130\,\mathrm{km/h} on a road, next to a train with v_T = 80\,\mathrm{km/h} on the track below; a bracket of 1500\,\mathrm m is drawn between them. Next to it: "SOLVE AT HOME" and the hint

s_x = v_x\cdot t + s_0
Symbols
  • s_x — position along the road/track (m); v_x — the constant speed of the car or the train (m/s); s_0 — its position at t = 0 (m)
  • v_C, v_T — speeds of the car and the train (km/h; divide by 3.6 for m/s)

The hint is the constant-acceleration law with a = 0: both vehicles drive at constant speed, so there is no t^2 term, and each gets one equation. The method, without the board's numbers so the exercise stays yours: convert both speeds to m/s; put the origin at a convenient place (e.g. the car at t = 0); write s_C(t) = v_C\,t + s_{C0} and s_T(t) = v_T\,t + s_{T0}; "has overtaken" means the two fronts are level, so set the positions equal and solve for t; insert t to get the distance.

Unclear (p. 7): what the 1500 m is

The sketch draws the 1500 m bracket under the car and above the train, so it is either the train's length or the head start the car has to make up. The board gives no question text. Both readings are solved the same way; only s_{T0} changes.

Worked example — overtaking with different numbers

A car at 100\,\mathrm{km/h} passes a truck at 80\,\mathrm{km/h}; it has to gain 50\,\mathrm m. How long does it take, and how far does the car drive?

  1. Convert: 100/3.6 \approx 27.78\,\mathrm{m/s}, 80/3.6 \approx 22.22\,\mathrm{m/s}.
  2. One equation per vehicle (car starts at 0): s_C = 27.78\,t, s_T = 22.22\,t + 50 (m, with t in s).
  3. Same position: 27.78\,t = 22.22\,t + 50, so t = 50/5.556 = 9.0\,\mathrm s.
  4. Distance: s_C = 27.78 \cdot 9 = 250\,\mathrm m (the truck meanwhile drives 200\,\mathrm m).
  5. Shortcut, relative motion (section 6): seen from the truck, the car closes the gap at 5.556\,\mathrm{m/s}, giving the same 9\,\mathrm s in one step.

3 Free fall

Lecture: p. 2 ("Free fall", cliff example), p. 4 (Torricelli, 16 Oct) · Giancoli §2-7

Near the Earth's surface, a body that is only acted on by gravity (no air resistance, no engine) falls with a constant acceleration, the same for every body: free fall. As a vector:

\vec g = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ -9.81 \end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}
Symbols
  • \vec g — gravitational acceleration as a vector (m/s²); the z-axis points up, so its z-component is negative
  • g = \lvert\vec g\rvert \approx 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2} — its magnitude

Video (link on the board): Brian Cox visits the world's biggest vacuum | Human Universe - BBC — BBC.

In air, the feather is slowed by air resistance much more than the stone, relative to its weight, so it lags. Remove the air and both fall together: in free fall the acceleration is the same for every mass, which is why no mass appears in any free-fall formula. Since \vec a = \vec g is constant, section 1 applies, one coordinate at a time.

Example: a stone thrown up from a cliff

Given: \vec v_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 15 \end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{m/s}, \vec s_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{m}, \vec g = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -9.81 \end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}, t_0 = 0\,\mathrm s.

The example uses two coordinates (horizontal, vertical), so \vec g has two components. The stone is thrown straight up at 15\,\mathrm{m/s} from the origin at the cliff edge, rises, turns, falls back past the edge and lands at the bottom, 50 m below the start. The question implied by the picture: when does it hit the bottom, and how fast is it then?

The board writes the integrals of section 1 with arrows (each component is integrated on its own):

\vec s(t) = \underbrace{\vec s(t_0)}_{\vec s_0} + \int_{0\,\mathrm s}^{t} \vec v(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau, \qquad \vec v(t) = \vec v_0 + \int_{0\,\mathrm s}^{t} \vec a\,\mathrm{d}\tau = \vec v_0 + \vec g\,t
\vec s(t) = \vec s(t_0) + \int_{0\,\mathrm s}^{t} \bigl(\vec v_0 + \vec g\cdot\tau\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}\tau = \vec s_0 + \vec v_0\,t + \tfrac12\,\vec g\,t^2
Symbols
  • \vec s(t) — position vector (m); \vec s_0 = \vec s(t_0) — its starting value; \vec v_0 — starting velocity (m/s)
  • \vec v(t) — velocity (m/s); \vec a = \vec g here (m/s²); t — time since the throw (s); \tau — integration variable (s)

Two curved arrows under the last line show which term becomes which: \vec v_0 \to \vec v_0\,t and \vec g\,\tau \to \tfrac12\,\vec g\,t^2. The stone reaches the bottom at the time t_c:

\vec s(t_c) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -50 \end{pmatrix}\mathrm m = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\mathrm m + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 15 \end{pmatrix}\mathrm{m/s}\cdot t_c + \frac12\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -9.81 \end{pmatrix}\mathrm{m/s^2}\cdot t_c^2
Symbols
  • t_c — time at which the stone reaches the bottom (s)
  • (0, -50)\,\mathrm m — the bottom's position: 50 m below the start, straight below it, since y points up

A vector equation is two equations. The x-equation reads 0 = 0 for every t_c and says nothing; the y-coordinate carries the information:

-50\,\mathrm{m} = 15\,\mathrm{m/s}\cdot t_c + \tfrac12\,\bigl(-9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\bigr)\,t_c^2

Symbols as above. "\Rightarrow solve for t_c \Rightarrow t_{c1} = 5.07\,\mathrm{s}, t_{c2} = -2.01\,\mathrm{s}." The algebra the board skips (units dropped inside, t in s):

\begin{aligned} 4.905\,t_c^2 - 15\,t_c - 50 &= 0 && \text{(}\tfrac12 \cdot 9.81 = 4.905\text{; all terms to one side)} \\ t_c &= \frac{15 \pm \sqrt{15^2 + 4 \cdot 4.905 \cdot 50}}{2 \cdot 4.905} && \text{(quadratic formula, coefficients } 4.905,\ -15,\ -50) \\ &= \frac{15 \pm \sqrt{1206}}{9.81} = \frac{15 \pm 34.73}{9.81} && \\ t_{c1} &\approx 5.07\,\mathrm s, \qquad t_{c2} \approx -2.01\,\mathrm s && \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. The motion starts at t = 0, so only t_{c1} = 5.07\,\mathrm s is physical. At t_{c2} the parabola y(t) also passes -50\,\mathrm m, but that is the formula extrapolated to before the throw. The velocity at the bottom:

\vec v_c(t_c) = \vec v_0 + \vec g\cdot t = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 15 \end{pmatrix}\mathrm{m/s} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -9.81 \end{pmatrix}\mathrm{m/s^2}\,\bigl(5.07\,\mathrm{s}\bigr) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -35 \end{pmatrix}\mathrm{m/s}
Symbols
  • \vec v_c(t_c) — velocity at the bottom (m/s); 5.07\,\mathrm s — the physical root t_{c1}

The y-component is 15 - 9.81 \cdot 5.07 = -34.7\,\mathrm{m/s}, rounded on the board to -35\,\mathrm{m/s}; units \mathrm{m/s^2} \cdot \mathrm s = \mathrm{m/s} ✓; the minus sign means downward. Two checks: the time-free law vertically gives v_y^2 = 15^2 + 2(-9.81)(-50) = 1206, so \lvert v_y\rvert \approx 34.7\,\mathrm{m/s} ✓ (the same \sqrt{1206} as in the quadratic formula); and the story: the stone rises for 15/9.81 \approx 1.53\,\mathrm s to 15^2/(2 \cdot 9.81) \approx 11.5\,\mathrm m above the edge, turns, and falls 61.5\,\mathrm m to the bottom.

Common mistake — the acceleration at the top is not zero

Throw a ball up at 12\,\mathrm{m/s}. At the highest point (t \approx 1.22\,\mathrm{s}, about 7.34\,\mathrm{m} up) the velocity is 0, but \vec a = \vec g the whole time: the velocity is changing there, from up to down, at the same rate as everywhere else. If \vec a were \vec 0 at the top, the ball would hover. Related: on the way up, velocity and acceleration point in opposite directions, so they need not point the same way. And with "up" positive, the vertical component of \vec g is -9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}, not +9.81.

The Torricelli equation

From the 1D time-free law v_1^2 = v_0^2 + 2as (section 1), the special case v_0 = 0\,\mathrm{m/s} gives v_1^2 = 2as, or v_1 = \sqrt{2as} (positive root, a speed).

Board sketch: red axes with x pointing down and y to the right; \vec g pointing down; a mass m starts at rest ("v_0 = 0\,\mathrm{m/s}") and falls the height H (dashed line with an arrow).

With the axis pointing down, the acceleration is a = +g and the displacement s = +H, both positive, so no signs need juggling:

\boxed{\,v_1 = \sqrt{2gH}\,} \quad\to\ \text{"TORRICELLI EQUATION"}\ \text{(1D)}
Symbols
  • v_1 — speed after falling the height H from rest (m/s)
  • g \approx 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2} — gravitational acceleration, positive here because the axis points down
  • H — height fallen (m); m — the mass (kg), drawn but absent from the result

The speed after a free fall depends only on the height, not on the mass and not on the time it took. Four times the height gives twice the speed. Units: \sqrt{\mathrm{m/s^2} \cdot \mathrm m} = \mathrm{m/s} ✓.

Worked example — dropping from 20 m

A tool falls from rest from a 20\,\mathrm m high platform. How fast is it at the ground?

  1. Check the conditions: starts from rest, only gravity acts, a height is given and no time → Torricelli.
  2. Insert: v_1 = \sqrt{2 \cdot 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2} \cdot 20\,\mathrm m} = \sqrt{392.4}\,\mathrm{m/s} \approx 19.8\,\mathrm{m/s}.
  3. Cross-check via the time: H = \tfrac12 g t^2 gives t = \sqrt{2H/g} \approx 2.02\,\mathrm s, and v = g t \approx 19.8\,\mathrm{m/s} ✓.
Problem-solving steps — free fall
  1. Choose the vertical axis and say which way is positive; put the origin at the start.
  2. Write \vec g with the matching sign (-9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2} if up is positive).
  3. Use the constant-acceleration laws for the vertical coordinate; a horizontal coordinate (if any) has zero acceleration.
  4. "Highest point" means vertical velocity 0; "hits the ground" means the vertical position equals the ground's (often negative) coordinate.
  5. Keep the root that fits (t > 0); check with the time-free law or Torricelli.

4 Variable acceleration: back to the integrals

Lecture: p. 1 ("1D"), general formulas · Giancoli §2-8

The general formulas at the top of section 1, v(t) = v_0 + \int_{t_0}^{t} a(\tau)\,\mathrm d\tau and x(t) = x_0 + \int_{t_0}^{t} v(\tau)\,\mathrm d\tau, hold for any acceleration, not only a constant one. When a depends on time, integrate it step by step; the constant-acceleration formulas then no longer apply.

Worked example — integrating twice, and what a changing a does

Same start for both: x_0 = 1\,\mathrm{m}, v_0 = 2\,\mathrm{m/s}, t_0 = 0. Case A: constant a = 1.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}. Case B: a ramp, a(t) = 3 - t (in \mathrm{m/s^2}, t in s). Find v and x at t = 3\,\mathrm{s}.

  1. Velocity = start + area under a–t: A: v = 2 + 1.5\,t, so v(3\,\mathrm{s}) = 6.5\,\mathrm{m/s}. B: v = 2 + 3t - \tfrac12 t^2, so v(3\,\mathrm{s}) = 2 + 9 - 4.5 = 6.5\,\mathrm{m/s}. Different histories, same area (4.5\,\mathrm{m/s}), same velocity at the end.
  2. Position = start + area under v–t: A: x = 1 + 2t + 0.75\,t^2, so x(3\,\mathrm{s}) = 13.75\,\mathrm{m}. B: x = 1 + 2t + 1.5\,t^2 - \tfrac16 t^3, so x(3\,\mathrm{s}) = 1 + 6 + 13.5 - 4.5 = 16\,\mathrm{m}.
  3. Why they differ: in B the velocity rises fast at first, so the body was faster during most of the 3 s and covered more ground.
  4. Trap: plugging B's average acceleration (1.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}) into x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2 gives 13.75\,\mathrm{m}, which is wrong for B. That formula needs a constant a.

5 Uniformly accelerated motion in vector form

Lecture: p. 4 ("16.10.2026") · Giancoli §3-6

In two or three dimensions the same laws hold for each coordinate. The board writes them as one vector law:

\boxed{\,\vec s(t) = \vec a\cdot\frac{t^2}{2} + \vec v\cdot t + \vec s_0\,} \quad\to\ \text{UNIFORMLY ACCELERATED (+/-) MOTION}

with an arrow from \vec s to "\vec x, \vec y, \vec z, \vec r, \vec p".

Symbols
  • \vec s(t) — position vector at time t (m); any of the position letters \vec x, \vec y, \vec z, \vec r, \vec p
  • \vec a — the constant acceleration vector (m/s²); "(+/−)": it may speed the motion up or slow it down
  • \vec v — the velocity at t = 0, i.e. \vec v_0 (m/s); the board drops the index here
  • \vec s_0 — position at t = 0 (m); t — time since the start (s)

It is the boxed x(t) of section 1, as a vector and highest power first. Uniformly accelerated means \vec a is constant in size and direction. A vector equation is three ordinary ones, one per coordinate, each with its own a, v_0, s_0. Watch the dropped index: here \vec v means \vec v_0, not the current velocity.

The board compares it with a parabola from maths:

y = ax^2 + bx + c, \qquad y(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \quad\to\ \text{in our case } x \to t, \qquad \vec s = \begin{pmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \\ z(t) \end{pmatrix}
Symbols
  • maths: a, b, c — coefficients of a parabola in the variable x
  • physics: x(t), y(t), z(t) — the coordinates of \vec s as functions of time (m)
maths: y = a x^2 + b x + cphysics: s = \tfrac{a}{2}\,t^2 + v_0\,t + s_0
variable xtime t
a (coefficient of the square)\tfrac12 \times the acceleration
bstarting velocity v_0
cstarting position s_0

Careful: the letter a means two different things in the two columns. Each coordinate is a parabola in t, or a straight line if that component of \vec a is zero.

The sign of the acceleration component decides which way the parabola opens: negative → opens down (like x(t): thrown up, rises, peaks, falls); positive → opens up (like y(t)). The vertex is where that velocity component is zero. In z(t) the vertex touches the axis: the body is at z = 0 exactly when its z-velocity is zero, e.g. a body starting from rest at the origin, z = \tfrac12 a_z t^2.

Common mistake — reading the x–t graph as the path

A parabola in an x–t graph does not mean the body moves on a curved path. A stone thrown straight up moves on a vertical line, yet its height–time graph is a parabola. The path is what you get by plotting the coordinates against each other (y over x), with t eliminated (6 Projectile Motion).

6 Relative motion

Lecture: p. 3–4 (class exercise 2) · Giancoli §3-9

Positions, velocities and accelerations are always measured from some reference. Seen from a moving point P_1, another point P_2 is at the relative position x_{2/1} = x_2 - x_1; differentiating gives the relative velocity and acceleration, v_{2/1} = v_2 - v_1 and a_{2/1} = a_2 - a_1.

Class exercise 2

Task (sheet): The motion laws of two points P_1 and P_2 moving along the direction x are, respectively: x_1(t) = 3 + 5t and x_2(t) = 0.5 + 2t^2. Determine the physical quantities describing the relative motion of P_2 with respect to P_1 and compute the relative motion law. Then describe the motion.

The board attaches the units that make each term a length (3 in m, 5 multiplies a time so m/s, 2 multiplies a time squared so m/s²):

x_1(t) = 3\,\mathrm m + 5\,\mathrm{m/s}\cdot t, \qquad x_2(t) = 0.5\,\mathrm m + 2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\cdot t^2

With P_1 as reference:

x_{2/1}(t) = x_2(t) - x_1(t) = -2.5\,\mathrm m - 5\,\mathrm{m/s}\cdot t + 2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\cdot t^2
v_{2/1}(t) = -5\,\mathrm{m/s} + 4\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\cdot t, \qquad a_{2/1}(t) = 4\,\mathrm{m/s^2}
Symbols
  • x_1(t), x_2(t) — positions of P_1 and P_2 on the x-axis (m); t — time (s)
  • x_{2/1}(t) — relative position of P_2 with respect to P_1 (m): where P_2 is, seen from P_1; negative = behind P_1
  • v_{2/1} = \dot x_{2/1} — relative velocity (m/s); a_{2/1} = \dot v_{2/1} — relative acceleration (m/s²)

Step by step: (0.5 + 2t^2) - (3 + 5t) = -2.5 - 5t + 2t^2 (the bracket's minus flips +5t); differentiating gives -5 + 4t (constant → 0, -5t \to -5, 2t^2 \to 4t), and once more 4. This has the form x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2 with x_0 = -2.5\,\mathrm m, v_0 = -5\,\mathrm{m/s}, a = 4\,\mathrm{m/s^2}: seen from P_1, P_2 performs a uniformly accelerated motion.

"Then describe the motion" (not on the board). P_2 starts 2.5\,\mathrm m behind P_1 and at first falls further behind, because P_1 is faster (v_{2/1} < 0). At t = 1.25\,\mathrm s the relative velocity is 0 (both equally fast) and the gap is largest, x_{2/1} = -5.625\,\mathrm m. After that P_2 is faster, closes the gap and passes P_1 where x_{2/1} = 0: 2t^2 - 5t - 2.5 = 0 gives t = \frac{5 + \sqrt{45}}{4} \approx 2.93\,\mathrm s (the other root is negative). Then it pulls ahead with growing relative speed.

Video (link on the board): Levin2.mp4 (AAU Seafile).

Common mistake — subtracting the wrong way round

"P_2 with respect to P_1" means x_2 - x_1: the reference point is subtracted. Swapping the order flips every sign (x_{1/2} = -x_{2/1}) and turns "P_2 is behind" into "P_2 is ahead".

Problem-solving steps — relative motion on a line
  1. Write both motion laws with units, from the same origin and the same clock.
  2. Subtract the reference body's law: x_{2/1} = x_2 - x_1.
  3. Differentiate for v_{2/1} and a_{2/1}.
  4. "Largest gap" → v_{2/1} = 0; "meet / pass" → x_{2/1} = 0, keep the root with t > 0.
  5. Interpret signs: negative relative position = behind the reference.
